tip: 'Kloppen' literally means to knock, but 'het klopt' means that is correct. 'Het klopt niet' means that is not right.
Regular verbs form the past with '-te' or '-de'. 'Koken' becomes 'kookte', giving the simple past she cooked.
In the perfect tense split verbs put 'ge-' in the middle: 'opmerken' becomes 'opgemerkt', not 'geopmerkt'.
For equal comparisons Dutch uses 'zo ... als': 'zo eenvoudig als' means as simple as.
With 'al' plus the present tense, 'wachten al een half uur' means have been waiting half an hour and still are.
'Zitten' plus 'te' plus an infinitive says someone is busy doing something: 'zit ... te werken' means is sitting working.
'Zich zorgen maken' is a set phrase for worrying. The command keeps the 'je': 'maak je geen zorgen'.
Some verbs change their vowel in the past instead of adding an ending: 'zingen' becomes 'zong', plural 'zongen'.
The ending '-je' makes a small or fond version of a noun: 'dorp' becomes 'dorpje', a little village.
Dutch usually picks a position verb by shape. Upright things 'staan', so the monument 'staat op het plein' rather than 'is'.
'Hoeven' means need to and shows up mainly in the negative, usually paired with 'te': 'zij hoeft zich nergens ... te maken'.
'Bang' takes 'voor' for what you fear: 'bang voor spinnen' means afraid of spiders.
Putting the object first flips subject and verb: 'een interessant boek lees ik', with 'lees' before 'ik'.
'Op straat' = on the street – no article in this fixed phrase.
Events and occasions usually take 'op', not 'in': 'welkom op het feest', like 'op school' or 'op een bruiloft'.
Greetings fuse into one word: 'goede' plus 'morgen' give 'goedemorgen', like 'goedemiddag' and 'goedenavond'.
'Niet' moves to the end to negate the verb when the object is definite: 'geloven dat verhaal niet'.
'Er' with a verb states existence: 'is er nog plaats' = is there still room?
'Nog geen' = not yet any – 'nog' (still/yet) stacks onto 'geen' (not any).
After 'een' before a het-word, the adjective drops the '-e': 'een nieuw begin', but 'het nieuwe begin'.
To agree, Dutch uses the fixed frame 'het ermee eens zijn'; negation splits it: 'het er niet mee eens'.
After 'terwijl' the verb goes to the end of its clause: 'terwijl de kinderen slapen'.
'Opkomen' is a split verb, so in a main clause 'op' moves to the very end: 'de zon komt ... op'.
'Las' is the simple past of 'lezen'; this form suits a repeated past habit: 'ik las elke avond'.
The present passive uses 'worden' plus a past participle: 'wordt ... geopend' = is being opened.
Front a time phrase and the verb still stays second, so the subject follows it: 'na het ontbijt lees ik'.
Dutch uses the present with 'al' for duration where English says have known: 'die ik al twintig jaar ken'.
Before a comparative, 'nog' means even: 'nog moeilijker' = even harder.
'Logeren' is to stay over temporarily, not to live; the host takes 'bij': 'logeren bij vrienden'.
This is the split verb 'afslaan'; the command splits it and 'rechts' slots in: 'sla ... rechtsaf'.
